newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Newcrest says MD John Quinn resigns.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Newcrest says MD John Quinn resigns.

text.p: Gold miner Newcrest Mining Ltd said on Wednesday that managing direCtor John Quinn had resigned due to differences with the board.
The company said it had appointed former CRA Ltd group executive Ian Johnson as chief executive.
Newcrest, whose main mining interests are located at Telfer in the Western Australia goldfields and Cadia Hill in New South Wales, has seen its share price decline sharply in recent months.
From a high of A$5.40 a share on February 5, Newcrest shares have fallen steadily, closing trading on Tuesday at A$3.21, the lowest since September 1993.
Under Quinn's direction, Newcrest attempted to be included in a complex merger of the rival gold miner Normany Mining Ltd's group in February 1996.
The bid failed, leaving Newcrest with an unwanted 11.9 percent stake in Normandy.
A statement issued by Newcrest said only that the resignation resulted from "differences" between Quinn and the board.
Quinn had been with the Newcrest group for 27 years, the statement said.
A search for a new long-term managing director has been started, the statement said.
Newcrest recently posted a net loss of A$7.1 million for the three months to March 31 and forecast a small full year loss before abnormals.
The resignation and interim naming of Johnson were effective immediately, Newcrest company secretary Bernard Lavery said.

Newcrest appeared to have recovered from the Normandy debacle by late February 1997, when a deal was structured enabling Newcrest to swap its Normandy stake with ANZ Bank for 740,000 ounces of gold at A$450 an ounce, raising A$337.225 million.

Newcrest's real benefit from the deal, however, would come only if the gold price approached A$500 an ounce. The precious metal currently fetches only about A$450 an ounce.
Early reaction to the resignation and appointment of Johnson was positive for Newcrest's share price, which at 0055 GMT (10.55 a.m.) was trading 21 cents up at A$3.42 a share.
Newcrest also has suffered from an unexpected loss of gold production this year from its Telfer mine in Western Australia, owing to heavier-than-normal rainfall at the mine site.
The rains were forecast to reduce the mine's output by between 35,000 and 50,000 ounces in the 1996/97 financial year.
